title: She died at the San Diego border. A surveillance camera was in plain sight
gist: Graciela Gómez Hernández died in September 2025 in the Otay Mountain Wilderness one mile from a General Dynamics surveillance tower with cameras rated to track targets 5 to 7 miles away; a Times of San Diego analysis found at least 138 migrants died within nominal range of California border towers from 2022 through 2025, and MIT Technology Review's terrain analysis put at least 81 of them in a camera's clear field of view. The reporting documents broken hardware, unproven efficacy and migrant route displacement as the tower network triples toward 2,300 units by 2034.

insights.claim: A Times of San Diego analysis counted at least 138 migrants whose remains were found between 2022 and 2025 within the nominal range of a California border surveillance tower, and a separate terrain analysis concluded at least 81 of those people were most likely in a camera's unobstructed field of view.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Hard denominator for the efficacy debate: the systems' own advertised coverage brackets the deaths, so range is not the excuse.
insights.quote: From 2022 through 2025, Times of San Diego’s analysis found that at least 138 people died within the nominal range of a nearby surveillance tower.
insights.locator: About Times of San Diego’s report

insights.claim: Deaths near towers span sudden events like falls from the border wall and drownings as well as dozens of slow deaths of exposure that emergency aid could plausibly have averted, meaning the response window in many cases was hours or days rather than seconds.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Distinguishes detection failure from response failure — the slow-death cases are the ones that indict the alert-to-response chain, not the sensor.
insights.locator: Some of these migrants died swiftly

insights.claim: The tower nearest one documented death was a General Dynamics unit in place since 2019 carrying two sets of electro-optical and infrared cameras able to track targets 5 to 7 miles away, while the person lay one mile from it.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Specifies the gap between advertised optical capability and delivered outcome at a named installation — the kind of detail that drives contract scrutiny.
insights.quote: boasts two sets of electro-optical and infrared cameras with long-range lenses that can track targets 5 to 7 miles away
insights.locator: That tower, made by General Dynamics and in place since 2019

insights.claim: Proximity to death sites leaves only two possibilities, both of which are system failures: the network did not detect people in distress, or it detected them and officials offered no response.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: A clean binary for evaluating surveillance procurement claims — neither branch supports the life-saving marketing pitch.
insights.quote: Either the system didn’t detect these people in distress, or it did detect them—and officials offered no response.
insights.locator: The proximity of so many deaths to high-resolution cameras

insights.claim: An internal memo obtained by NBC News in October 2024 showed 30% of older operator-monitored towers were broken, mostly missing parts or running outdated unusable equipment, leaving roughly 150 non-functioning towers standing at the border.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Sustainment and spares, not new sensors, are the real bottleneck — relevant to anyone modeling service revenue versus unit sales in border tech.
insights.quote: These 150 broken towers still stood at the border, acting as million-dollar scarecrows.
insights.locator: An internal memo obtained by NBC News in October 2024

insights.claim: A March 2026 US military report on an installation of seven G-BOSS(E) towers in the Otay Mountain Wilderness described combat-grade systems that were vulnerable to tipping over, rodent damage, exhaust blowouts and battery depletion, with one truck-mounted tower's cameras left stuck in a zoomed-in position after a rough dirt road transit.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Field reliability of rugged-terrain claims is materially worse than datasheets imply; a durability risk for mobile surveillance vendors.
insights.quote: The combat-grade military surveillance towers were vulnerable to tipping over, damage from rodents, exhaust blowouts, and running out of battery.
insights.locator: In a report published in March 2026

insights.claim: The Electronic Frontier Foundation's director of investigations argues none of the tower systems have been shown effective because there is no independent evaluation of how much they actually capture.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Absence of independent benchmarking is the core asymmetry: vendors publish detection counts, nobody publishes miss rates.
insights.quote: None of these systems have been effective. There’s no independent evaluation of how many things they’re capturing
insights.locator: Dave Maass, the director of investigations

insights.claim: Surveillance at the border extends well beyond towers to trail cameras, underground movement detectors, radar, infrared sensors, drones, blimps, camouflaged cameras hidden in rocks and bushes, license-plate readers stuck to safety cones, and since a March 2025 directive, Department of Defense satellites.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: The addressable spend is a layered sensor stack, not just towers — satellite tasking and ground sensors are adjacent budget lines.
insights.locator: The towers are not the only form of surveillance in the region

insights.claim: The Government Accountability Office reported in June 2026 that Border Patrol had 803 fielded towers and planned to deliver another 175 across the southwestern border in an initiative costing $1.4 billion, with the tower count expected to reach 2,300 by 2034.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Sizes a near-tripling of the installed base over eight years — a durable order book for whoever holds the tower contracts.
insights.quote: the Border Patrol currently has 803 fielded towers “and plans to deliver another 175,” across the southwestern border, an initiative that would cost $1.4 billion
insights.locator: Officials from the Government Accountability Office wrote in a report in June 2026

insights.claim: Border Patrol expects roughly a billion dollars in border-technology funding from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed in 2025, on top of existing tower budgets.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Legislated funding, not annual appropriations discretion, is what underwrites the deployment curve — it is insulated from budget fights.
insights.locator: The report also notes that the agency expects a billion dollars in funding

insights.claim: Anduril makes about half of the towers now installed at the US-Mexico border and said in June 2026 that its installations had autonomously identified hundreds of thousands of border crossings.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Quantifies incumbent share in the AI tower segment and the detection-count metric the company chooses to publicize.
insights.quote: autonomously identified hundreds of thousands of border crossings
insights.locator: Anduril, the company that makes about half the towers

insights.claim: California's border towers are on a refresh cycle rather than a one-time build: towers have been in the area since 2011, AI-directed towers arrived in 2018, many current AI towers appeared in 2021, they were updated with longer ranges in 2026, and agents replaced dozens of cameras with new AI models this year.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Recurring upgrade revenue on an installed base is the more valuable business than initial tower placement — model it as a refresh cycle.
insights.locator: Surveillance towers have been in the area since 2011

insights.claim: Even where AI towers make up over half the network and can identify migrants autonomously, apprehensions still require human labor, so agent headcount rather than sensor coverage sets the effective throughput of the system.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Automation of detection without automation of response shifts the bottleneck downstream — buyers of these systems will need more staff, not fewer.
insights.locator: And though the manufacturer says the AI-enabled towers

insights.claim: A CBP official told RAND analysts that smugglers began sending migrants across alone rather than in groups specifically to flood surveillance towers with individual targets, generating more alerts than agents could follow.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Adversarial adaptation converts better detection into alert saturation — a structural limit on any sensor-led enforcement strategy.
insights.locator: A CBP official told the RAND analysts that smugglers began sending migrants

insights.claim: Agents routinely decline to pursue lone crossers because apprehending one person is not considered worth the time, according to a researcher who compiles migrant remains data, meaning solo travelers in distress are the least likely to be intercepted.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Explains why detection statistics and rescue outcomes diverge — the response function is selective by group size.
insights.quote: Even one person who’s not sick, one person who is just hiking on their own, often Border Patrol will just ignore them because it’s not worth their time to just only catch one person
insights.locator: So it is possible the towers in the vicinity did capture footage

insights.claim: A search and rescue group leader says Border Patrol agents told his volunteers they do not have the opportunity or time to conduct searches, and he believes some towers are 'just adornment' rather than effective tracking tools.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Frontline testimony that the deployed capability is partly symbolic, directly contradicting official situational-awareness claims.
insights.locator: Rafael Hernández Larraenza, the leader of a search and rescue group

insights.claim: RAND analysts wrote in 2020 that the outcomes and outputs indicating surveillance tower success are not directly observable, and that the likely deterrent effect on crossings through surveilled areas overwhelms any boost to situational awareness the towers provide.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: If the value is the threat signal rather than the sensing, capability upgrades may be economically irrelevant — a fundamental challenge to the AI-tower investment case.
insights.quote: The likely deterrent effect on migrant crossings through surveilled areas overwhelms any boost to situational awareness
insights.locator: Analysts from the RAND Corporation

insights.claim: Increasing surveillance density has historically pushed migrants into further, more extreme routes where searchers have very little hope of finding them, converting detection coverage into displaced mortality.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: The second-order effect that never appears in program metrics: coverage relocates risk rather than reducing it.
insights.quote: People are crossing through areas that are further out and more extreme, where we have very little hope of finding them in a search
insights.locator: Due to increased surveillance

insights.claim: As hundreds of new towers thin out the spaces outside detection range, migrants are increasingly choosing to sprint through surveilled territory rather than around it — running past sensors and not stopping to drink water in the roughly 15 minutes before agents arrive — which a researcher predicts will raise deaths in coming years.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Saturation flips migrant behavior from avoidance to speed, a mechanism that would make deaths rise even as crossings fall.
insights.quote: It seems like people aren’t stopping to drink water. People are going really fast, often running even, moving much more quickly, not being able to take the time to take care of themselves.
insights.locator: Peterson, the No More Deaths map-maker, said more migrants could die

insights.claim: Migrants often deliberately cross during the hottest weeks of the year in the belief that fewer agents will be patrolling, trading heat-death risk for lower apprehension risk.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Enforcement intensity and seasonal mortality are linked, so death counts respond to patrol patterns as much as to weather.
insights.locator: Larraenza says for this same reason

insights.claim: A migrant paid 20,000 pesos, about $1,150, for route knowledge alone with no guide and with her phone pinging her location back to smugglers in Tijuana, against a current average smuggling price of about $12,000.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Smuggling has tiered pricing where the cheapest tier strips out the guide — the discount product carries the mortality risk.
insights.locator: Gómez Hernández paid 20,000 pesos

insights.claim: Border crossings and reported deaths have decreased since January 2025, but consumption of water and supplies left on humanitarian routes has fallen in the Otay Mountain Wilderness while rising on other routes, indicating migration patterns are shifting rather than stopping.
insights.speaker: Lillian Perlmutter
insights.so_what: Route-level demand signals from aid-drop consumption offer a leading indicator that headline encounter numbers miss.
insights.locator: In the first half of 2026, fewer people have consumed the water bottles
